summary: The exam uses ICAO's definitions exactly. Know the aerodrome areas (manoeuvring area excludes aprons, movement area includes them), the declared distances (TODA = TORA + clearway, ASDA = TORA + stopway), and the vertical words (altitude from sea level, height from a datum, elevation of a point on the ground, flight level on 1013.2 hPa). A cloud ceiling is the lowest layer below 20,000 ft covering more than half the sky. A CTR starts at the surface, a CTA above it. Flight time runs from first moving to take off until coming to rest. The emergency phases are uncertainty, alert and distress.
sections: ICAO Annex terminology
Terms used in the ICAO Annexes and in the PPL exams, grouped by theme. See also the Part-FCL terms in Pilots Licences.
Aircraft
Aircraft: any machine that can derive support in the atmosphere from the reactions of the air, other than reactions against the earth's surface (so not a hovercraft).
Heavier-than-air: lift mainly from aerodynamic forces.
Lighter-than-air: supported mainly by buoyancy.
Aeroplane: power-driven, heavier than air, lift from fixed wings.
Glider: the same but not power-driven.
Rotorcraft: power-driven, lift from one or more rotors.
Helicopter: lift and control from power-driven rotors on substantially vertical axes.
Gyroplane: lift from a freely rotating rotor, thrust from a propeller.
Airship: power-driven lighter than air.
Balloon: non-power-driven lighter than air.
Aerodromes
Aerodrome: a defined area on land or water for the arrival, departure and surface movement of aircraft.
Heliport: the same for helicopters.
Aerodrome elevation: the elevation of the highest point of the landing area.
Aerodrome reference point: its designated geographical location.
Aerodrome traffic: all traffic on the manoeuvring area and all aircraft in the vicinity, which means in, entering or leaving the traffic circuit.
Manoeuvring area: used for taxiing, take-off and landing, excluding aprons.
Movement area: the manoeuvring area plus aprons.
Apron: for parking, loading, refuelling and maintenance.
Aircraft stand: a parking place on the apron.
Runway: a defined rectangular area for take-off and landing.
Threshold: the beginning of the usable runway (normally the piano keys).
Touchdown zone: just beyond it, where landing aircraft first touch down.
Taxiway, taxi-holding position (where you may be held before entering or crossing a runway), holding bay.
Signal area: where ground signals are displayed.
Marking: a symbol on the movement area surface.
Marker: an object above ground showing an obstacle or boundary.
Runway guard lights: warn that you are about to enter an active runway.
Aerodrome beacon: shows the aerodrome's location from the air.
Identification beacon: flashes a code to identify the location.
Hazard beacon: marks a danger.
Obstacle: any fixed or mobile object on the movement area, or one that sticks up through a protected surface, above a defined height.
Declared distances
TORA (take-off run available): runway length available for the ground run.
TODA (take-off distance available): TORA + clearway.
ASDA (accelerate-stop distance available): TORA + stopway.
LDA (landing distance available): runway available for the landing ground run (may start at a displaced threshold).
Clearway: an area beyond the runway, under the aerodrome's control, suitable for the initial climb.
Stopway: a prepared area beyond the runway for stopping after an abandoned take-off.
The CAA agrees declared distances; they are published in AIP AD.
Heights and levels
Altitude: vertical distance of a point from mean sea level.
Elevation: of a point on the earth's surface from mean sea level.
Height: from a specified datum (e.g. the aerodrome).
Level: a generic term for height, altitude or flight level.
Flight level: a surface of constant pressure related to 1013.2 hPa, in hundreds of feet (FL180 = 18,000 ft on 1013).
Pressure altitude: altitude in the standard atmosphere for that pressure (1013.2 set).
Transition altitude: at or below it, vertical position is by altitude (QNH); 3,000 ft at most UK aerodromes outside CAS, higher in some CAS (18,000 ft in the USA).
Transition level: the lowest flight level usable above it.
Transition layer: between the two.
Cruising level: held for a large part of the flight.
Weather and visibility
Cloud ceiling: height above ground or water of the base of the lowest layer below 20,000 ft covering more than half the sky.
Visibility: how far prominent unlit objects by day and lit objects by night can be seen.
Flight visibility: forward from the cockpit in flight.
Ground visibility: at an aerodrome, reported by an observer.
Runway visual range (RVR): how far a pilot on the centreline can see the runway markings or lights.
VMC: visibility, cloud distance and ceiling equal to or better than the minima.
IMC: less than them.
SIGMET: hazardous weather information for flights. AIRMET (now GAMET in the UK) for low-level flights.
Meteorological report: observed conditions at a place and time.
Forecast: expected conditions.
Air-report: a report from an aircraft in flight.
Slush: water-saturated snow that splatters underfoot.
Dry snow: blows when loose, falls apart when squeezed.
Wet snow: sticks into a snowball.
Compacted snow: pressed into a solid mass.
ATS and airspace
Air traffic service: flight information, alerting, air traffic advisory or air traffic control service.
Air traffic control service: to prevent collisions (in the air, and on the manoeuvring area with obstructions) and expedite an orderly flow.
ATC clearance: authorisation to proceed under conditions set by ATC.
ATC instruction: a directive requiring a specific action.
Clearance limit: the point the clearance runs to.
Flight information service: advice and information for safe and efficient flight.
Alerting service: notifies organisations of aircraft needing SAR, and assists them.
Control zone (CTR): controlled airspace from the surface up to a specified limit.
Control area (CTA): controlled airspace from a specified height above the surface.
Terminal control area (TMA): a control area normally around major aerodromes.
Airway: a control area in the form of a corridor.
Controlled airspace: ATC is provided to IFR and VFR flights in line with its class.
Controlled aerodrome: ATC is provided to aerodrome traffic (not necessarily inside a CTR).
Controlled flight: any flight subject to an ATC clearance.
Advisory airspace / advisory route: air traffic advisory service available (none in the UK now).
Flight information region (FIR): FIS and alerting available.
Flight information centre: the unit that provides them.
ATS unit: ATC unit, flight information centre or ATS reporting office.
Special VFR flight: a VFR flight cleared by ATC to operate in a control zone in conditions below VMC.
Traffic information: from ATC about known traffic nearby.
Traffic avoidance advice: advice to help avoid a collision.
ATIS: continuous recorded broadcast of routine aerodrome information.
Holding fix (the book calls it a "holding point"): a location around which an aircraft flies a standard holding pattern. In UK radio a holding point is the place you stop before a runway.
Expected approach time: when ATC expects a holding aircraft to leave the hold for its approach.
Approach sequence: the order of aircraft cleared to approach.
Radar
Primary radar: uses reflected radio signals.
Secondary surveillance radar (SSR): an interrogator prompts a reply from the aircraft's transponder.
Radar contact: the aircraft's position seen and identified on the display.
Radar identification: positively identified by the controller.
Radar vectoring: headings given from radar.
Radar monitoring: radar used to tell aircraft about deviations from their route or clearance.
ACAS: airborne collision avoidance from transponder signals, independent of the ground.
Flight plans and times
Flight plan: specified information given to ATS about an intended flight.
Filed flight plan: as submitted, before any changes.
ETA: VFR, arrival over the destination aerodrome; IFR, arrival over the point where the instrument approach begins.
Estimated off-block time: when the aircraft will start moving for departure.
Estimated elapsed time: from one significant point to another.

Flight time: the total time from when the aircraft first moves for the purpose of taking off until it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight ("chock to chock"). The book says "from the beginning of the take-off roll", which contradicts its own note.
Pilot-in-command: responsible for the operation and safety of the aircraft during flight time.
Operator: a person or organisation engaged in aircraft operation.
Alternate aerodrome: where you can go if landing at the destination becomes impossible or inadvisable (en-route or destination alternate).
Emergencies, accidents and SAR
Emergency phase: uncertainty, alert or distress phase.
Uncertainty: safety uncertain.
Alert: concern for safety.
Distress: reasonably certain of grave and imminent danger or need of immediate assistance.
Ditching: a forced landing on water.
Accident, serious incident, serious injury: see Accident Investigation Regulations.
Rescue coordination centre: organises SAR in a search and rescue region.
Rescue unit: trained and equipped people.
Dangerous goods: articles or substances that pose significant risk to health, safety or property when carried by air.
Fireproof material: withstands heat as well as or better than steel.
States
State of Registry: where the aircraft is registered.
State of the Operator: the operator's principal place of business. State of Design and State of Manufacture: responsible for the type design and final assembly.
State of Occurrence: where the accident or incident happens.
Appropriate authority: over the high seas, the State of Registry; over a State's territory, that State.
Communications
Blind transmission: sent when two-way contact can't be made but the station is believed to receive it.
Broadcast: an "all stations" transmission.
Aeronautical fixed service: between fixed points (e.g. the AFTN).
Aeronautical station: a ground or sea station in the aeronautical mobile service.
Location indicator: the four-letter code of an aeronautical fixed station (e.g. EGKK).
Air-taxiing: a helicopter moving above an aerodrome surface, normally in ground effect, below 20 kt groundspeed.

sum.ICAO Annex terminology: The definitions the exam uses, grouped by theme.
sum.Aircraft: Lighter or heavier than air, power-driven or not: aeroplane, glider, helicopter, gyroplane, airship, balloon.
sum.Aerodromes: Manoeuvring area excludes aprons; movement area includes them. Elevation is the highest point of the landing area.
sum.Declared distances: TORA; TODA = TORA + clearway; ASDA = TORA + stopway; LDA.
sum.Heights and levels: Altitude from MSL, height from a datum, elevation of a ground point, flight levels on 1013.2 hPa.
sum.Weather and visibility: Ceiling: lowest layer below 20,000 ft covering more than half the sky.
sum.ATS and airspace: CTR from the surface, CTA from a height above it; a clearance authorises, an instruction directs.
sum.Radar: Primary radar uses reflections; SSR gets replies from transponders.
sum.Flight plans and times: Flight time runs chock to chock; ETA for VFR is over the destination aerodrome.
sum.Emergencies, accidents and SAR: Uncertainty, alert and distress phases; ditching is a forced landing on water.
sum.States: State of Registry, of the Operator, of Design, of Manufacture and of Occurrence.
sum.Communications: Blind transmission, broadcast, location indicators (EGKK) and air-taxiing.

cards.a: For taxiing, take-off and landing, excluding aprons.
The elevation of the highest point of the landing area.
All traffic on the manoeuvring area and all aircraft in the vicinity (in, entering or leaving the circuit).
Vertical distance of a point from mean sea level.
Vertical distance from a specified datum.
Vertical distance of a point on the earth's surface from mean sea level.
The lowest flight level available above the transition altitude.
Base of the lowest layer below 20,000 ft covering more than half the sky.
CTR from the surface up; CTA from a specified height above the surface.
A clearance authorises you to proceed under conditions; an instruction directs a specific action.
A VFR flight cleared by ATC to operate in a CTR below VMC.
From first moving for the purpose of taking off until coming to rest after the flight.
Withstands heat as well as or better than steel.
Helicopter movement above an aerodrome surface, normally in ground effect, below 20 kt groundspeed.

quiz.q: The movement area of an aerodrome is:
o: The manoeuvring area plus the aprons
The manoeuvring area, excluding aprons
The runways only
The aprons and taxiways only
quiz.why: Movement includes aprons; manoeuvring excludes them. The exam swaps these often.

o: TORA plus clearway
TORA plus stopway
TORA plus stopway plus clearway
The landing distance available
quiz.why: Clearway is for the climb-out, so it extends the take-off distance. Stopway extends ASDA.

o: TORA plus stopway
TORA plus clearway
TODA plus stopway
The runway length less any displaced threshold
quiz.why: Accelerate-stop: you need somewhere to stop, so stopway.

quiz.q: Aerodrome elevation is the elevation of:
o: The highest point of the landing area
The notified aerodrome reference point
The threshold of the main instrument runway
The base of the aerodrome control tower
quiz.why: ICAO uses the highest point of the landing area.

quiz.q: The vertical distance of an aircraft from mean sea level is its:
o: Altitude
Height
Elevation
Flight level
quiz.why: Altitude is from MSL. Height is from a datum such as the aerodrome; elevation is for a point on the ground; flight levels use 1013.2 hPa.

quiz.q: A cloud ceiling is the height of the base of the lowest cloud layer:
o: Below 20,000 ft covering more than half the sky
Below 10,000 ft covering more than half the sky
Below 20,000 ft covering at least a quarter of the sky
Of any amount below 5,000 ft
quiz.why: More than half the sky (BKN or OVC) and below 20,000 ft.

quiz.q: A control zone is controlled airspace extending:
o: Upwards from the surface to a specified upper limit
Upwards from a specified height above the surface
From FL100 up to FL195, around major aerodromes
Along a corridor between radio navigation aids
quiz.why: A CTR starts at the surface. A CTA starts at a height above it; an airway is a corridor-shaped CTA.

quiz.q: Under ICAO and Part-FCL, flight time starts when the aircraft:
o: First moves for the purpose of taking off
Begins its take-off roll on the runway
Becomes airborne at the end of the take-off run
Has its engine started for the flight
quiz.why: It runs from first moving to take off until it comes to rest. The book's glossary says 'take-off roll', which is wrong.

o: The lowest flight level available for use above the transition altitude
The highest altitude that may be flown with QNH set on the altimeter
The airspace between the transition altitude and the transition level
Always FL40 in the UK, whatever the transition altitude is locally
quiz.why: The transition altitude is the top of QNH flying; the transition level is the lowest usable FL above it; between them is the transition layer.

quiz.q: An area at the end of the runway prepared for stopping after an abandoned take-off is a:
o: Stopway
Clearway
Runway end safety area
Holding bay
quiz.why: Stopway is for stopping (in ASDA). Clearway is for the initial climb (in TODA).
